articles.title: North America’s biggest book sorter just opened in the Seattle area
articles.author: Ken Yeung
paras: Washington is home to Mount Rainier, the Space Needle, and the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks . It’s also now home to what the King County Library System says is North America’s largest library materials sorter — a $5.2 million installation in Renton that formally opened Wednesday to handle the 25,000 items circulating through KCLS’s 50 libraries every day.

The new warehouse has been running since June 14. It’s the culmination of a more than three-year process. It replaces KCLS’s previous distribution center in Preston that operated for almost 25 years. Heidi Daniel , the organization’s executive director, said it was time to modernize: “It couldn’t keep pace with our growing community.”

In 2025, KCLS’s 700,000-plus active cardholders checked out more than 11 million physical items and 12 million digital items. And while the previous sorter “served KCLS faithfully,” it was plagued by mounting maintenance needs and frequent breakdowns. “We were literally ordering parts off of eBay,” Daniel said.
KCLS said the new sorter can handle up to 8,000 items per hour at full tilt.

Warehouse operations manager Charlie Mitchell walked through the sequence: drivers returning from branch pickups load totes onto one of two conveyor belts, and a pair of robotic arms at the far end destack them at a rate of one every 15 seconds.

On an average day, Mitchell estimated that 800 to 900 totes could be received. A human worker scans each item individually, and that scan tells the system where the material goes next: onto a second belt and into one of 186 chutes where it’s packaged into a new tote for the next delivery run.
Rest assured, these books aren’t being destroyed after being scanned.

It took KCLS nearly four months to set up and install everything. The facility is run by a team of 13 people — six tasked with scanning library materials and seven who manage the back end, ensuring the new totes are filled and then setting them aside while they await delivery.
When asked if it was challenging to train on the new equipment, Mitchell said no: “It’s a good job to pick up on.”

The clearest gains of this new setup, he said, are for the people working around the machine. Totes used to stack 14 levels high, sending workers up ladders to reach them; the new setup tops out at five, and instead of pushing totes down the line by hand, staff pulls them off onto a hand truck.
The noise level dropped too. “The old system ran at about 89 decibels,” Mitchell said. “This [new sorter] runs at 67 decibels. It’s about the same as a vacuum cleaner.”

The other payoff shows up at the branches. Mitchell explained that the old sorter ran at 2 to 3 mph and put books in the wrong bin 1% to 2% of the time. While a low percentage, it sparked uncomfortable conversations with patrons who received an email saying their book was available for pickup. The new machine features automated tracking and destination redundancy support, likely reducing the odds of any mis-sorting.

King County Councilmember Steffanie Fain said the new facility solves a “major flaw” in the library system — at least according to her two young children: It will enable books to move through the system faster so people won’t have to wait as long anymore for the material they want to read, listen, or watch.
“I’m not sure my kids have ever had an opinion about a distribution center before, but this one definitely has their full support,” she said.

“Today isn’t just about unveiling a remarkable piece of technology,” Daniel said. “It’s about investing in the future of KCLS, and most importantly, it makes a promise to the 1.6 million residents we are proud to serve: No matter where you live or which library you visit, you get the same selection, the same service, and the same speed.”

As a child, Analía Azic used to pretend she was secretly a princess, the heiress to a magical distant kingdom. In real life, she was the daughter of a greengrocer named Juan Antonio Azic and a demure housewife named Esther Abrego. The family lived in the province of Buenos Aires, which, as anyone from the area will tell you with a dash of pride, is not the city of Buenos Aires but its rougher neighbour. Analía was not royalty, but she had an iron will and audacity out of proportion to her small stature.

Analía cared little for grades at the Ladies Institute of the Sacred Heart, where she rolled with the dominantes , girls who hiked their school skirts up so high they served as little more than belts, and dreamed of the weekend when they could finally trade in their school uniforms for designer jeans and tight tank tops and sashay into Electric Circus, the one local club that allowed in minors. There, Analía would climb atop the speakers and dance, then leap back down to toy with the boys from the Argentine air force’s technical trade school.

paras: This punishingly hot and dry summer will probably be followed by another wet winter. But it’s nothing compared with what Britain will endure in years to come

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales is in drought, while key reservoirs are parched. Across this brown and stickily unpleasant land, from Grimsby down to St Ives, hosepipe bans are in force , while music festivals are staged not on green fields but in giant dust bowls.
Just how bad is it? I asked a leading climate scientist.

paras: Prof Gustaf Hugelius warns wildfires could accelerate release of methane and carbon as vast regions approach irreversible thresholds

This is a major concern for Gustaf Hugelius, a professor at the Bolin Centre of Climate Research at Stockholm University, Sweden, and a leading authority on the risks from thawing tundra and peatlands. In this Q&A, he explains why the world should pay attention.

articles.title: Qualtrics cuts jobs in Seattle, Utah and overseas as it absorbs $6.75B acquisition
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Three months after closing its $6.75 billion purchase of Press Ganey Forsta, Qualtrics is cutting jobs across the combined company — a reduction that the experience-management technology company says reflects duplication between two organizations that were built independently.

The cuts are global, including the company’s dual headquarters in Seattle and Provo, Utah, and its international offices. Qualtrics is not publicly disclosing how many jobs were cut, and did not break out numbers by office, region, or job function.

One clue: Qualtrics sent impacted Seattle employees layoff notices under the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, or WARN, according to one copy reviewed by GeekWire. The notice covers workers at Qualtrics Tower, 1201 Second Ave., its Seattle headquarters.

The Washington law applies only to layoffs of 50 or more at one site — so at least that many jobs were cut at the Seattle HQ. As of publication time, Qualtrics had not appeared in the Washington or Utah state WARN databases, which can sometimes lag the notices to employees by a day or more.
Individual employees learned their status by email Wednesday morning.

In a memo to employees, obtained by GeekWire, Qualtrics CEO Jason Maynard called the acquisition a “defining milestone” for the company but said it “meant making hard decisions about what the organization needed to operate and function as a single uniform team.”

“Since the acquisition closed, we’ve gone function by function, team by team, to understand where we have overlap and determine what we needed to do to move forward as one company,” he wrote, noting that the decisions were “made based on the structure of our combined organization: the roles we need, the capabilities we are building toward, and where we have duplication.”
Qualtrics makes software that companies use to collect, analyze, and adapt to feedback from customers and employees, a category of technology that it branded “experience management.”

Current and former employees posting publicly Wednesday on LinkedIn and other forums described cuts spanning departments and offices, including Seattle, Provo and international locations, and hitting both the legacy Qualtrics and Press Ganey Forsta sides of the business.

The Press Ganey Forsta acquisition, announced in October and completed in May, added what Qualtrics called the largest healthcare experience dataset in the industry. Press Ganey Forsta, based in Indiana, was itself the product of earlier mergers, and its Forsta products competed directly with Qualtrics.

The cuts follow a leadership shakeup in April , when Maynard removed five senior executives and outlined a broader reorganization spanning marketing, customer operations, IT and corporate development. Maynard, who joined from Oracle , became CEO in February.

It’s not the first round of cuts under private equity ownership. Qualtrics cut about 780 jobs, roughly 14% of its workforce , in October 2023 under then-CEO Zig Serafin, who cited complexity from years of rapid hiring. It had cut about 270 jobs earlier that year.

Qualtrics has been owned by private equity firm Silver Lake and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board since 2023, when they acquired it for $12.5 billion . It was the second time the company changed hands in under five years, following SAP’s $8 billion acquisition in 2019 and a 2021 IPO .

articles.title: Want to know what Jeff Bezos brings to Liverpool FC? Study Amazon’s Leadership Principles
articles.author: John Cook
paras: What does Jeff Bezos’ new ownership stake in English Premier League powerhouse Liverpool FC mean for the storied soccer club?
I was invited by Dan Clubbe of the Liverpool fan site The Redmen TV to talk about the Amazon founder’s recent investment, Bezos’ first real foray into sports ownership.
Across the 45-minute discussion, I shared thoughts about Bezos’ transformation from the nerdy, khaki-wearing entrepreneur of his early career to the higher-profile “ Buff Bezos ” of the past decade.

On the surface, it appears as if Bezos will, for now, take an arm’s-length approach to Liverpool. He’s investing through a consortium , 1892 Holdings, that owns about a 38% interest in the team and an option to buy it outright.

One point I made: Bezos leads a very busy life. The sci-fi nerd’s true passion is his space company, Blue Origin, and he is also spending considerable time as the co-CEO at newly formed AI startup Prometheus . And with a new wife (Lauren Sanchez Bezos, who seems to be the true sports fan between them) there may not be enough hours in the day for the Miami resident to worry much about the inner workings at Anfield.
But Bezos does bring enormous capital and business acumen to the team.
To better understand what this might mean for Liverpool, I suggested Clubbe and his mighty team of reporters take a closer look at Amazon’s famous Leadership Principles .

Some of the most relevant Leadership Principles include “Ownership,” which asks leaders to think long term and not trade lasting value for a quick result; “Customer Obsession,” which means starting with what the customer wants and working backward; and “Insist on the Highest Standards,” setting the bar higher than most people think reasonable.
That said, the Amazon principle of “Frugality” doesn’t really play well these days on the world soccer stage.

We talked about the changing nature of global soccer, driven by big personalities and big money, and the balancing act it takes to build a soccer club while respecting the community of fans. I noted how this tightrope was a hard one for Bezos to walk in terms of his relationship to Amazon’s hometown of Seattle, something that might give Liverpool fans pause.

articles.title: Internal memo: Eight execs out at Expedia Group in AI-driven shakeup
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Expedia Group is parting ways with at least eight vice presidents and senior vice presidents in a major reorganization designed to reorient its product and technology groups around AI.

In an internal memo Tuesday, obtained by GeekWire, the Seattle-based online travel giant’s top product and technology leaders said “AI has radically changed what’s possible” over the past year, and that “work that once took weeks increasingly happens in hours.”

The company must “fundamentally change how we work, how we’re organized, and the technology we build,” wrote Chief Product Officer Shilpa Ranganathan and Chief Technology Officer Ramana Thumu in the memo (full text below).
They said the company is moving to “small end-to-end squads with clear ownership” and making AI and machine learning “part of every mission.”

This comes amid the online travel industry’s broader reckoning with the implications of artificial intelligence. AI agents are emerging as a new interface for travel, with the potential to relegate booking platforms to inventory sources behind the scenes unless they keep pace.
Expedia confirmed the departures in response to an inquiry from GeekWire.

“We’re evolving our Product and Technology organization to better align engineering and product teams with the brands and businesses they support,” an Expedia Group spokesperson said via email. “By bringing teams closer to the work and decisions, we can move faster and deliver more impactful experiences for travelers and partners.”

The spokesperson described the impact as “limited,” not saying how many roles were cut. “The majority of the changes involved employees moving to different teams or changes in reporting lines to better align talent and resources with business priorities,” the spokesperson said.
Most of the changes are to leadership scope and reporting lines, according to the memo, but “in a small number of cases, we made the tough decision to eliminate some roles.”

Reorg details: The most senior departure is Sachin Singh , SVP of book-to-trip technology, a former Amazon exec who joined Expedia in 2022 and served on the CTO leadership team. The memo credits him with advancing priorities “across checkout, payments, fraud prevention, servicing, and AI.”

Singh’s portfolio is being broken up. According to his LinkedIn profile, he led checkout, payments, fraud and risk, and post-booking self-service. The memo moves fraud and risk under Chief Information Security Officer Hilik Kotler , self-service under Ryan O’Neill , and payments product, technology and operations under Reena Patil and Debashis Saha .

Seven other leaders are also leaving, according to the memo: Sara Beckmann , Ian Butcher , Matt Esler , Amitabh Ghosh , Emil Riccardi , Fiona Stevenson and Shao Xie . Their LinkedIn profiles list them as vice presidents in product and technology roles including pricing, lodging, data platform, and travel platform and fraud.

The memo also lists promotions. Saha was elevated to senior vice president of travel foundations. Four leaders were promoted to vice president: Rajat Arora , Ryan Hillman , Ashwita Kaur and Ambrish Srivastava . All four were senior directors, according to their LinkedIn profiles.
Data, AI and agentic platforms all move under Xavier Amatriain , the former Google AI executive Expedia named as its first chief AI and data officer in December.
Rick Fast , senior vice president of platform engineering, becomes chief architect.

A third disruption for travel: In a May interview marking the company’s 30th anniversary, Expedia Group CEO Ariane Gorin described artificial intelligence as the third major technology disruption in Expedia’s history, after the internet and mobile. She said the AI era was “only starting to unfold.”

The online travel industry is facing the prospect that AI assistants could do to Expedia and Booking.com what those companies once did to traditional travel agents — inserting themselves between travelers and suppliers, and pushing the incumbents into the background. Marriott’s CEO has said AI booking agents will hurt online travel agencies more than they will hotels.
Expedia has been embedding itself in the new platforms as a hedge. It was a launch partner when OpenAI opened ChatGPT to outside apps, and began buying ads inside ChatGPT this year.

So far the disruption has moved slower than feared. When OpenAI pulled its Instant Checkout button from ChatGPT’s main interface in March and stepped back from processing travel transactions directly, shares of Expedia and Booking Holdings jumped significantly.
Expedia Group’s brands include Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo, along with Orbitz, Travelocity, ebookers and Wotif, plus its majority-owned hotel metasearch subsidiary, trivago.

The company ended 2025 with about 16,000 employees across nearly 50 countries, according to its most recent annual report, and said “approximately one half of our people work in technology roles” — putting the organization at the center of Tuesday’s memo at roughly 8,000 people.
Employment peaked above 25,000 in 2019, fell to 14,800 during the pandemic, and rebounded to 17,100 by the end of 2023, before a series of restructurings and layoffs in recent years.
We’re making some organizational changes to bring our teams closer together.

Our mission is to grow our business and build a platform that propels both our consumer and B2B businesses forward. To do this, we need to move a lot faster, and, over the past year, AI has radically changed what’s possible. Work that once took weeks increasingly happens in hours. To fully realize that opportunity, we must fundamentally change how we work, how we’re organized, and the technology we build. As we work differently, we will move faster from idea to outcome, organize into small end-to-end squads with clear ownership, make AI and Machine Learning part of every mission, and build products that scale.

Several teams have been piloting a different way of working that removes the usual constraints and provides squads and smaller cross-functional teams clear ownership. Our new structure considers what these teams have learned, that:
Going forward, you should expect less time coordinating and waiting, and more time working together to build great experiences for travelers and partners.

Most changes are to leadership scope and reporting lines, bringing teams closer and simplifying our organization. In a small number of cases, we made the tough decision to eliminate some roles. Anyone experiencing a change directly has been informed.
Detailed placemats are posted on Basecamp, but some of the key changes are:
Experience Design under Rachel Been has made some adjustments to enable tighter alignment with our Product and Technology teams.

With this, Sachin Singh will be leaving Expedia Group. During his time on the CTO Leadership Team, we advanced key priorities across checkout, payments, fraud prevention, servicing, and AI that have had a real impact for travelers and the business.

We also want to recognize Sara Beckmann, Ian Butcher, Matt Esler, Amitabh Ghosh, Emil Riccardi, Fiona Stevenson, and Shao Xie, who will be leaving Expedia Group, and thank them for their leadership and contributions.

Additionally, Debashis Saha has been promoted to SVP, Travel Foundations and the following leaders have been promoted to Vice President: Rajat Arora, Ryan Hillman, Ashwita Kaur and Ambrish Srivastava.

Your leaders will be reaching out and hosting team meetings soon to walk through more context, org charts, and questions. In the meantime, head to Basecamp for more, including domain placemats, team charters, and more details.

This new structure is one step. The real work is in how we operate within it. It’s a new chapter for our teams as we deepen the partnership between Product and Technology and go after our big bets with speed and focus. We’re excited about what’s ahead, and we hope you will be too as you learn more about what this means for your day-to-day,

articles.title: TikTok cuts 75 jobs in Seattle area, hitting e-commerce teams
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: TikTok is laying off 75 workers in the Seattle region, focused largely on the company’s e-commerce business, according to a notice filed Tuesday with Washington state.

Job titles listed in the notice are almost entirely TikTok Shop and Global E-Commerce roles in Bellevue, Wash., including anti-fraud and governance program managers, seller and creator operations staff, campaign managers, data scientists, and backend and frontend engineers.

It’s part of a steady stream of tech layoffs this year. Zillow cut more than 500 jobs this month, including 91 in Washington state. Microsoft eliminated 605 positions in the state in July as part of a broader reduction of 4,800. Google cut 52 jobs and Salesforce cut 59 locally this month.

The notice Tuesday was filed by TT Commerce & Global Services LLC on TikTok letterhead, and lists two ByteDance employees as contacts. It gives the affected facility as Lincoln Square North at 700 Bellevue Way NE, with a separation date of Oct. 19.

TikTok Shop is the company’s in-app shopping business, which lets brands and creators sell products directly in TikTok videos and livestreams. The company has used the Seattle region as a base for the e-commerce push, expanding its Bellevue offices as it built out the business.
GeekWire has contacted TikTok representatives for comment, and asked for details on the size of the company’s remaining workforce in Bellevue and the Seattle region.
The cuts follow TikTok’s announcement on Aug. 6 that it will close its Nashville office and lay off all 250 workers there, most of them on content moderation teams.
The company last year cut 65 Seattle-area jobs , including 38 at TikTok and 27 at ByteDance.

articles.title: Zeno Power reserves a spot on Firefly moon lander to demonstrate its atomic space heater
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: A nuclear-powered heater built by Zeno Power Systems is slated to fly to the moon aboard Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost lunar lander for a demonstration mission that could take place as early as 2028.

Zeno’s Seattle engineering hub played a leading role in developing the radioisotope heater unit, which will be powered by americium-241, a radioactive isotope typically recovered from recycled nuclear material.

The unit will provide 5 watts of thermal energy — enough to sustain the payload during the lunar night, which lasts 14 Earth days. Firefly’s first solar-powered Blue Ghost lander, which touched down on the moon in March 2025, operated successfully through the lunar day but gave up the ghost shortly after sunset.

“Our first Blue Ghost mission gave us firsthand insight into the moon’s extreme thermal environment, where we measured temperatures ranging from more than 230 degrees F during the lunar day to below -275 degrees F at night,” Ray Allensworth, Firefly’s vice president of spacecraft, said today in a news release . “Now we’re looking forward to advancing technologies that can extend missions beyond sunset and support long-duration surface operations required for NASA’s Moon Base initiative and the growing lunar economy.”

The lander will rely on solar power to run NASA-funded science payloads on the moon’s near side during the lunar day. When night falls, Zeno’s payload will go into operation and transmit data back to Earth.

“Hardware capable of surviving the extreme cold of the lunar night will be essential to enabling sustained operations on the moon,” said Tyler Bernstein, CEO and co-founder of Zeno Power. “NASA’s Moon Base program has identified the need for technologies such as radioisotope power systems to support future lunar exploration, and Zeno is proud to answer that call to demonstrate this capability aboard Firefly’s Blue Ghost mission.”

Firefly has two other lunar lander missions on its manifest: a trip to the moon’s far side scheduled for no earlier than 2027; and a mission targeting a region known as the Gruithuisen Domes , set for 2028 or later.

Beyond radioisotope heater units, Zeno is developing radioisotope power generators to supply electricity for missions on the moon and in extreme environments on Earth. “As demand for long-duration lunar infrastructure grows, we are building the production capacity to support future commercial and government missions,” Bernstein said.

In addition to its Seattle engineering hub, Zeno maintains facilities in Washington, D.C. , and California . The company reported the completion of a $50 million Series B funding round in May , followed by a $3.6 million funding extension from Seraphim Space.

“Zeno has raised $105 million to date in private investment and has 95 employees,” Kelsey Bates, the company’s communications manager, told GeekWire in an email. The Seattle hub accounts for the largest proportion of those employees.

articles.title: Sammamish Poised to Pivot Away from Town Center Growth This Fall
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Councilmembers in the sleepy Eastside bedroom city that is Sammamish face a crucial decision later this fall, in the wake of council elections that tilted the balance of power away from its previous pro-density direction. The impact of the decision will likely be felt for years to come, as city leaders decide whether to step away from a plan that was intended to finally foster the beleaguered Town Center area into something closer to a real downtown for a city of nearly 70,000.

Incorporated in 1999, Sammamish has been trying to foster some type of center city for its entire (albeit brief) existence. In 2008, after years of debate, the council approved a Town Center plan that capped development at 2,000 housing units, despite capacity for many more across 240 acres.

Very little of that plan, which envisioned separate mixed-use "nodes" far away from the main thoroughfare of 228th Avenue SE, came to fruition. One reason was very meager density limits, with developers like the builders of the Village at Sammamish Town Center (home to Metropolitan Market) consolidating their projects on a portion of a lot in order to be able to build up.

"When the Town Center was originally adopted, it was envisioned in part as a place to put the growth. However, the opposite, you could argue, actually happened, and instead of growth happening in the town center, the growth continued to happen as infill in the neighborhoods in the form of single-family residential subdivisions," Sammamish Community Development Director David Pyle said last month.

A few months before the November election, the Sammamish Council voted 6 to 1 to advance study of a growth alternative for Town Center that would have increased the upper limit on the number of units that could be built from 2,000 – where it has stood for nearly two decades – to 4,000. The move was intended to be a step toward creating development standards that allow a mixed-use neighborhood to take shape, rather than Sammamish's current glide path toward more townhouse development in the so-called city center.

Then the voters weighed in, sweeping two pro-density councilmembers out of office and tilting the balance of power away from the bloc that had voted yes last year. In a campaign season that had focused heavily on the Town Center issue, all three councilmembers who took office in January had opposed the idea of studying 4,000 units in explicit terms, citing issues like traffic, infrastructure costs, and "unchecked development."

Josh Amato, who was selected by the new growth-skeptical majority to be mayor in January, had included a banner at the top of his campaign website that read "Josh is opposed to the 4,000 unit upzone in the Town Center."

Now the city has to decide how to move forward, but doing nothing and fully abandoning the Town Center plan isn't an option. Without some density increases within the city, Sammamish doesn't have enough capacity for households across lower income bands, a directive spelled out in House Bill 1220 , which the state legislature passed in 2021.

Moreover, City leaders are eyeing the new Housing Accountability Act , in which the state's Commerce Department reviews the growth plans in select cities to make sure that they're in compliance, and they don't want to end up on the watch list alongside places like Carnation and Bainbridge Island . Before moving to pass an emergency ordinance to get into compliance, Bainbridge had been flirting with triggering the Builder's Remedy, which would have superseded local zoning to allow much greater height and density when builders include a set amount of affordable housing.

In July, city staff sought direction from the Sammamish Planning Commission, with commissioners expressing a clear interest in an "option 4" that would take planned capacity increases in Town Center and distribute that to the city's other commercial centers, like Klahanie, Pine Lake, and Inglewood.

"The biggest advantage of option four, is if you spread it over six or seven [...] different neighborhood centers or subareas, you distribute the traffic, which has been the major, major opposition of the community, going from 2,000 to 4,000, because the town center basically infrastructure is not there to support even the 2,000," commission vice chair Seyed Safavian said.
Safavian noted that Klahanie, currently home to a QFC grocery store, is well-positioned when it comes to a Sound Transit light rail station in Central Issaquah.

"Klahanie has perfect access, and within 5, 10 minutes... access to the freeway, access to the future transit, and Klahanie has really very good roads, road capacity, intersections, roadway improvement infrastructure, and all that that really helps us a lot as far as accepting more housing units, particularly for affordable housing," Safavian said.

Ultimately, it will be up to the Sammamish Council to decide how to proceed, with some moves this year signaling the new majority's potential direction. A unanimous vote last month removes a policy from the city's Comprehensive Plan that would have pushed the city to pursue a designation as a regional growth center, a move that could have unlocked more infrastructure funding for the city – and likely come with requirements for more density.

Just this week, the council voted 5-2 to overhaul its affordability requirements in low-density residential areas, essentially gutting a fee in-lieu program that was intended to act as something of a check on the city's continued proliferation of large single-family homes. Previously, all new homes over 1,500 square feet were required to pay a fee that would be used to fund affordable housing, but that threshold was raised to 1,750 square feet – with the fee only applying to square footage exceeding that threshold.
But the looming Town Center vote will likely be the most pivotal of the year, determining how Sammamish grows for at least a decade.

"Trying what we tried from before, we will end up with the same opposition that we faced from before. It's the same community, it's the same people. Let's try something different," planning commissioner Hisham Elkhawad said. "You said it needs more work. I would rather do the more work and succeed at the end of it instead of trying what we tried, and we failed."
Correction: an earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that three councilmembers lost their reelection bid last year, but the number is two: one seat was an open race.

articles.title: Op-Ed: How Pike Place Market Can Thrive in the Winter Without Car Traffic
articles.author: Gordon Padelford
paras: Seattleites love Pike Place Market, but hate random vehicle traffic pushing through the heart of it. That has been clear over and over again in surveys and polls, so it has come as a shock that the City is proposing to allow all car traffic Monday to Thursday from October through March .

The latest survey from the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), conducted this past June, heard from 5,403 people and found “98% Support: Near-universal community backing for vehicle barriers.” Importantly, the survey also heard “96% Business Agreement: High alignment among local merchants and staff” among 224 respondents.

Limiting general car traffic in the Market is as close to complete political consensus as Seattle is going to get on anything. Support spans the spectrum of Seattle politics from The Stranger and Mayor Wilson, to the Seattle Times and former Mayor Bruce Harrell.
And let’s be clear about what we’re talking about when we say “limiting general-purpose car traffic” or “pedestrianization.”

No one is seriously proposing preventing businesses from loading and unloading (regardless of whether businesses are using personal or commercial vehicles to do so), deliveries from reaching the Market, or emergency vehicles from responding when needed.

We’re talking about restricting unnecessary vehicle trips: tour buses, Ubers, lost tourists rubbernecking in rentals, and visitors who want to drive and park on the street for their personal convenience.
Limiting this unnecessary traffic makes Pike Place more functional, and makes room for what makes Pike Place special.

During the pilot, the Market has continued to function as both a loading dock and a front porch — a place where farmers can vend in the street, musicians can busk, visitors can sit and gather, and businesses can receive the deliveries they need to operate.
The good news is that, overall, the pilot has been successful :

But unfortunately there were never any agreed on success metrics for the pilot, so the debate about it seems to be endless and anecdotal. The latest news is a proposal to scale back the pilot to allow more vehicles on the street Monday through Thursday starting this fall through the early spring — why?

The issue seems to be that a subset of businesses say some of their driving customers are buying less because they find it inconvenient or expensive to park in the attached 800-stall public car parking garage ( Urban Freight Lab memo ). Exactly how many discouraged driving customers we are talking about is not clear. The Urban Freight Lab study found in a survey of 2,546 visitors to the Market that only 14.5% of customers drive (85.5% walk, bike, or take transit), but how many of those feel discouraged by having to park in the garage seems to be unknown — so we’re stuck with anecdotal concerns that seems to be driving this decision (pun intended).
The good news is that there are alternative solutions to retain these picky driving customers instead of opening Pike Place back up to general purpose traffic !

Taking this approach would make for a better shopping experience for the 85.5% of customers who don’t drive, and open up possibilities to grow the customer base even more. Last fall, we interviewed five pedestrianized markets in Cincinnati , Burlington , Boulder , Charlottesville , and London to learn how they stay active and vibrant all winter long. Here are a few possibilities inspired by those conversations:
Pedestrianization would also mean more space for vendors to safely load and unload on the street.
It would mean parents can shop with their children without worrying about random car traffic.
It would mean people with disabilities can walk or roll in the street without worrying about whether they will be seen by a backing-up tourist in a rental SUV.

It would mean that Pike Place is more than a parking lot — it’s both the loading dock and the front porch of the heart of Seattle. It’s a destination for the public to visit, shop, gather, and build community. It’s no wonder 98% of Seattleites want to keep it prioritized for people — the real question is why can’t our governance structures deliver a better Pike Place for everyone?

You can ask them by emailing your thoughts to: Pike Place Market Historical Commission MinhChau.Le@seattle.gov >, Pike Place Market Preservation and Development Authority (PDA) info@pikeplacemarket.org >, SDOT Director angela.brady@seattle.gov >, and Mayor of Seattle mayor.wilson@seattle.gov >.

articles.title: Lambert House ready to reopen renovated Capitol Hill LGBTQ+ youth center after two-year overhaul
articles.author: CHS
paras: Setting up for a past Lambert House Pink Prom (Image: Lambert House)

On August 31st, the Lambert House LGBTQ+ Youth Center will reopen its Capitol Hill headquarters on 15th Ave, resuming daily programming and hosting a housewarming family-style dinner in its renovated dining room. The reopening expands space for Seattle’s marginalized youth and marks a major milestone for LGBTQ+ youth centers nationwide.

“For youth who are growing up, hearing in news sources and news feeds every single day that they are the subject of tremendous public controversy and there’s a lot of people in the world that want them to disappear and not exist,” executive director Ken Shulman said. “Having a place like this as a refuge really matters.”

Leadership this summer completed a comprehensive renovation to update the century-old building, featuring a foundation rebuild, earthquake retrofitting, complete utility system updates, new bathrooms, and expanded spaces for the kitchen, dining room, art studio, and recreation areas.

For the past two years, the center operated out of temporary space at St. Mark’s on 10th Ave while the original building underwent these structural repairs and expansions. Despite the relocation, Lambert House maintained its full schedule of nightly dinners, support groups, game nights, and community activities. With renovations complete, Shulman announced it is time to return to their permanent home, where the upgrades directly serve the more than 700 youth who visit annually.

The physical improvements are critical to providing safety and security for visitors. Lambert House purchased its 15th Ave property in 2016, joining a select few independent LGBTQ+ youth centers that own their facilities.
“When [nonprofits] get far enough to the outskirts, their clients stop following them,” Shulman said.

“Having a space that’s only theirs [for LGBTQ+ youth] is part of providing them with the psychological and emotional safety that they need in order to get over all the stressors and the increased risks,” Shulman said.

Lambert House was founded in 1981 by Dr. Bob Deisher , a pediatrician who observed how social isolation harmed his LGBTQ+ patients’ health. After meeting in church basements and clinics for a decade, Lambert House leased the Victorian on Capitol Hill, creating the nation’s first community-based drop-in center for LGBTQ+ youth.

A decade ago , when the building’s landlords intended to sell, a longtime donor provided a zero-percent interest loan, enabling the organization to buy it. Through fundraising, corporate matching programs, and grants, Lambert House fully paid off its $2 million mortgage in 2024, clearing the way to complete the extensive structural upgrades. Revenue related to the Convention Center even went to help foot the bill.

“We’re going to be settling in for a while,” Shulman said about their quiet reopening, referring to setting up detailed areas like the new art studio. “I don’t mean in a general, big picture way … I mean the specifics,” he added. “Where do the shelves go and what goes on what shelf? That level of detail.”
Lambert House exclusively serves youth ages 10 to 22. Visitors under the age of 12 require parent or guardian permission.
The house was raised for foundation work (Image: Lambert House)

Shulman describes it as a controlled space where visitors interact only with vetted, trained volunteers. During orientation, new visitors share their goals; Shulman noted that 92 out of 100 kids write, “to make friends.” The newly enlarged recreational spaces and dedicated activity rooms were redesigned specifically to foster these social connections.

“Making friends during adolescence is preventive for depression that can lead to suicide and for using alcohol and other drugs as a coping mechanism for social isolation,” Shulman said about the “minority stress” many LGBTQ+ youth face when they are being bullied in school or experience fear and anxiety about coming out.
For everybody — LGBTQ+ and non-LGBTQ+ youth alike — teenage years are typically a time when kids find “self awareness”, Shulman said.

While the center provides essential sexual safety resources, Shulman notes that youth often gain their most meaningful insights into relationships and self-awareness through natural, open conversations with their peers.

“They’re talking about ‘who do you think is cute, who do you want to date, who are you dating, who is so-and-so dating,’” Shulman said. “Some people start earlier, some people start a little older. But that’s part of that time in life and it’s very important for them to be able to talk to each other about that.”
“We want kids to be able to educate each other and be able to talk openly with each other in frank, explicit, helpful ways to keep each other safe and healthy.”
There are also simpler conversations — like what’s for dinner.

A key area of improvement in the renovated house is the expanded dining room, which now doubles its previous seating capacity for weekday evening meals at 6 PM, where visitors serve themselves buffet-style and sit around one big dining table.
“The dining table is a very special place here,” Shulman said about the youth center’s community meals.

“We have kids from different backgrounds, different economic class backgrounds, different educational backgrounds, different religious backgrounds, who would never sit at the same table in the cafeteria at school,” Shulman said.
You can learn more about Lambert House at lamberthouse.org .

articles.title: ‘Biden hired me’ — Video reportedly shows Capitol Hill ICE activity as Seattle Times reports surge in arrests
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A video reportedly showing ICE activity on Seattle’s Capitol Hill this week and a testy exchange of words with one of the armed officers during an operation on 10th Ave E comes amid reports of a surge in federal immigration arrests in the region.

Recorded from the passenger seat of a vehicle traveling northbound along 10th Ave E, the video captures law enforcement activity from Tuesday in the residential neighborhood. The car moves slowly down the street, passing multi-story homes, landscaped yards, and several parked vehicles.
As the car passes a driveway, armed officers wearing tactical vests marked “POLICE ICE” are shown standing outside.

One officer in sunglasses, a ballcap, and a blue shirt is confronted by a man on foot who walks up filming with a smartphone, asking questions about family history escaping Nazi Germany and officer pay. The officer dismisses the questions, stating, “I’m not getting into this with you guys” before remarking, “Biden hired me. I don’t know what to tell you,” as a second officer in a full-face balaclava stands nearby.

The recording continues down the block, showing additional officers on the sidewalk alongside unmarked enforcement vehicles, including a dark Dodge Durango with active red and blue grille strobe lights and a plain white cargo van. The clip sent to CHS ends as the vehicle drives past local onlookers on the sidewalk and a residential yard sign that reads “ABOLISH ICE” with a handwritten note attached.
The video sent to CHS shows multiple ICE officers in position but does not show any arrests.
There have been other unconfirmed reports of ICE activities in the area including operations Wednesday morning again on Capitol Hill.

The Seattle Times reports an increase in public, broad-daylight ICE enforcement operations across Seattle during the summer following the Trump administration’s hiring of 12,000 more ICE agents since last July to meet a quota of 2,000 arrests a day across the U.S. set earlier this summer.
The Times reports videos circulating showing federal agents “detaining at least 10 people in separate daytime arrests since July 11” in areas across Seattle.

The ICE field office for Seattle continues to report updates on its operations including a bulletin Monday reporting the arrest of an alleged illegal alien from El Salvador who ICE said has convictions in Nevada and Oregon for “disturbing the peace, domestic violence/assault, a probation violation, and attempted to commit sex abuse.”
CHS has asked the Department of Homeland Security and ICE public affairs for more information on the Capitol Hill activities and any arrests.

articles.title: Proposal would ease building rules for neighborhood churches and daycares in Seattle multifamily zones
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The Seattle City Council is considering a bill to modify development standards for smaller institutional uses in multifamily zones throughout the city.

The legislation in front of the council’s land use committee Wednesday would make it easier for neighborhood organizations such as churches, temples, mosques, childcare facilities, and community centers to find new locations, build, or expand by allowing them to follow standard residential building rules rather than stricter separate regulations.
The proposal does not modify development standards, policies, or approval procedures for major institutions, such as hospitals, colleges, and universities.

Currently, institutional regulations in multifamily zones are more restrictive than those applied to less intense Neighborhood Residential zones. The new proposal is hoped to address this inconsistency by allowing qualifying institutions to adopt the same setback, height, structure width, and structure depth limits that govern regular residential developments in the same zone.
The bill would also remove buffers forcing institutions to stay at least 600 feet away from each other, while adding standard rules for greenery, landscaping, and screening around parking areas.
The Land Use and Sustainability Committee will hold a public hearing on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, at 9:30 AM on the proposal.

articles.title: Wilson recall effort moves toward August 31st public hearing
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The civil recall petition seeking to remove Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson has moved to the next phase after being officially assigned to King County Superior Court Judge Patrick Oishi .
This step is a formality as the court will now determine the validity of the case.

The process began when two Seattle voters filed recall charges alleging that Wilson has been derelict in her duties concerning public safety across the city. Under Washington state law governing recall efforts, the matter underwent a technical review by the Civil Division of the King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office . This preliminary evaluation checked the fundamental legal mechanics of the filing, verifying that the petitioners are registered Seattle voters, confirming the petition was properly signed, and ensuring the submission provided a concise summary of the claims.

Following this technical assessment, prosecutors submitted the formal Petition to Determine Sufficiency of Recall Charges and Adequacy of Ballot Synopses to the court, prompting the assignment to Judge Oishi.

An open public hearing is scheduled for Monday, August 31st 9:00 AM at the King County Courthouse . During this session, the court will not rule on the factual truth of the claims, but will determine whether the allegations legally meet the statutory criteria and whether the proposed ballot synopsis is sufficient to allow signature gathering to proceed.

State law requires collecting signatures equal to 25% of the total votes cast for all candidates in the preceding election for that office. Proponents would need to collect around 70,000 valid signatures in that scenario.
In 2021 , District 3 voters narrowly defeated a recall effort against City Councilmember Kshama Sawant .
The recall effort comes amid a spike in gun violence across Capitol Hill.

articles.title: Hunger Strike Over Poor Food Quality at NWDC Concludes
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: After nearly a week, more than 140 immigrants detained in the Northwest Detention Center (NWDC) have concluded their hunger strike in protest of inedible food, often served at irregular hours. The action marked the 20th hunger strike in the Tacoma facility this year.

Detainees in the center’s G3 unit began the protest last Tuesday, and were joined by detainees from the G4 unit the following morning. The participants then established contact with the immigrant solidarity group La Resistencia, which has relayed communications from detained migrants to the broader public.

According to La Resistencia, the meals at the facility are terrible and not nutritious. Receiving raw meat is not uncommon, and detainees have to rely on chips, ramen, and other processed food from the commissary—sold at exorbitant prices—to get by. Dinner is frequently served after midnight.
“Hunger strikes are often the only powerful tool that people have to be able to call to attention what is happening,” says La Resistencia director of organizing Josefina Mora-Cheung.

Days into the strike, participants entered into negotiations with employees of GEO Group, the private prison corporation which owns and operates the NWDC on behalf of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). According to a press statement by La Resistencia, the detainees stopped the hunger strike over the weekend after company representatives promised them new menus, improved food quality, and bigger portions.

The NWDC has been beset with allegations of poor conditions for many years. Researchers with the University of Washington Center for Human Rights have accused ICE and GEO Group of not only poor food but also denying immigrants access to proper health care while in custody and even failing to prevent or respond to sexual abuse within the facility. Under the second Trump administration, conditions have only deteriorated as the NWDC has been consistently overcrowded, with occupancy rates sometimes exceeding 90 percent of the center’s 1,575-person capacity.

In response to ICE’s crackdown on undocumented immigrants, protests against immigration detention have multiplied across the country . Mora-Cheung says the number of hunger strikes in the NWDC this year has already surpassed last year’s count of 16. ICE has been quick to retaliate against organizers like Cuban immigrant Rogelio Enrique Bolufé Izquierdo, who was deported to Ecuador shortly after he started a similar protest in late May.

Local and state leaders have also tried to intervene. In July, a federal judge sided with the Washington State Department of Health’s request to audit conditions within the detention center, a ruling which was later reversed by the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals.
Washington State and Oregon Congressmembers Representatives Emily Randall and Maxine Dexter showed up at a rally organized by La Resistencia on Saturday to lend their support for the hunger strike.

The NWDC’s status is currently up in the air after ICE did not renew its 10-year contract with GEO Group for the facility late last year, and instead opted for a short-term agreement. Randall suggested to KUOW that the move could be an effort by the federal government to enrich Trump allies like GEO Group founder and CEO George Zoley. In July, the private prison company CoreCivic sold two California detention centers to ICE for $1.5 billion .
In an email, ICE spokesperson Jason Chudy said any claims of “subprime conditions” in the NWDC were “FALSE.”
“All detainees are provided with 3 meals a day, an adequate supply of clean drinking water or other beverages, clothing, bedding, showers, soap, and toiletries,” Chudy wrote.
La Resistencia says that the detained immigrants were determined to strike again if the promised food improvements are not honored.
“Come to events like La Resistencia’s to show people on hunger strike that they’re not alone, because that’s what ICE and GEO [Group] continuously tries to make them believe,” Mora-Cheung said.

articles.title: Pop Loser: Courtney Love Update, New Shabazz Palaces Single, and Three Blood Brothers Return as Evil Island
articles.author: Dave Segal
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser. I’m Dave Segal and I’ll be filling in for Audrey Vann over the next three weeks. Not gonna lie: I generally don’t mess with pop music, but I am familiar with losing. So, the content of this column may hit a little differently than it does under Audrey’s byline; she has a mastery of the domain that I, a writer more than twice her age, could never match. However, I have had dalliances with pop during my Stranger tenure. Over the years, come late December, various sadistic editors would command that I write about the 10 or 20 most popular songs on Billboard ‘s year-end singles chart. I would do my best to complete the assignments with humor, insight, and snark. In retrospect, I should have filed an OSHA complaint. Anyway, let’s get on with the business at hand. Thanks for your tolerance during this difficult time.

Wait, Courtney Love almost died in 2020? Controversial leader of Hole and Kurt Cobain widow Courtney Love recently posted a video on Instagram in which she says she has completed a long-gestating solo album and is contemplating when and how to release the follow-up to her 2004 debut solo album, America’s Sweetheart . Among those who contributed to the new album are Echo & the Bunnymen’s Will Sergeant, Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong, former Hole bandmate Melissa Auf Der Mar, and Butch Walker. Also in the clip, Love discussed a terrifying illness that she experienced. “I went to England in 2019, and when I went there, you know, my body just exploded. It just exploded, and I was in hospitals a lot. I almost died. I lost all my hair. I was about 100 pounds, and they told me I was going to die, and I didn’t believe them.” In August 2020, Love was hospitalized with anemia, but she said she’s on the road to recovery with help from CBD, the miracle chemical.

Seattle’s preeminent hip-hop artist, Shabazz Palaces (basically now Ishmael Butler and Erik Blood), have just dropped a new single, “Ahh World (I Won the Alpha Bet).” It’s the first teaser from Shabazz Palaces’ eighth album, It’s a Style Sport , out October 23 on Sub Pop. “Ahh World” glides into earshot with an ominous rhythmic undertow, a slurred bass-synth riff, ruthless rimshots, and Ish’s flow of infinite cool and gravitas, as he intones autobiographical verses about what it took to ascend to the hip-hop summit. Along with Butler (aka Palaceer Lazaro) rapping and co-producing with Blood, guest musicians on the 10-track album include Marquette Miller, Thaddeus “Thaddillac” Turner, Evan Flory-Barnes, Gerald “Tugboat” Turner, Kassa Overall, and Carlos Overall. It’s nice to see that part of It’s a Style Sport was recorded at former Seattle producer Randall Dunn’s Circular Ruin Studio in NYC. Note: Shabazz Palaces are headlining The Stranger Genius Awards at the Moore Theatre on September 12, and Blood will be DJing the event as well.

The Blood Brothers’ vocalist Johnny Whitney has a new project called Evil Island. The Ross Robinson-produced debut album, Terraform the Afterlife , was released August 14 via Blowed Out Records. BB fans should dig the whirlwind of cathartic art-punk that Whitney and company are slinging here, though the songs are a bit more streamlined and accessible than the Brothers’. Drummer Mark Gajadhar and guitarist Cody Votolato of the Bros join Whitney, along with members of OFF!, …And You Will Know Us by the Trail of Dead, and Glassjaw. Also, Fugazi’s Guy Picciotto makes a cameo on one song. According to the press release, Whitney devised Evil Island as “a fictional nation ruled by the self-appointed overlord King Death, where AI, late-stage capitalism, corporate optimism, and political extremism have reshaped every facet of everyday life.” Skewering of authoritarianism and consumer culture in Whitney’s trademark strangulated yelp ensues. Evil Island play Linda’s Fest Aug 29.

RIP, respected music journalist Dave Marsh. One of the key writers and editors at influential Detroit music mag Creem, Dave Marsh, passed away on August 14 at age 76. He guided Creem (where I briefly worked as a proofreader and for which I freelanced in the mid ’80s) to prominence with its irreverent, incisive attitude toward rock during the publication’s early-’70s heyday. Marsh also authored several acclaimed books, including Before I Get Old: The Story of the Who , The Heart of Rock and Soul: The 10001 Greatest Singles Ever Made , and a surplus of tomes about Bruce Springsteen. On a personal note, many of Marsh’s reviews in The Rolling Stone Record Guide infuriated me so intensely that I couldn’t bring myself to read his books. Anyway, here’s Marsh on Kurt Cobain and the demands of musical “authenticity.”

The Boomer content you didn’t ask for : Have you seen the publicity shots for Sam Mendes’s The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event ? The actors playing John, Paul, George, and Ringo look like poor AI representations of the Fab Four. Filming began in March and the simultaneous release of all four biopics is scheduled for April 7, 2028. The fact that they couldn’t even get Lennon’s beard right does not bode well.

British trio Jungle (J Lloyd, Tom McFarland, and vocalist Lydia Kitto) deliver an absurdly cheerful tune that recalls “Since I Left You” by Australian sampledelic masters the Avalanches. If you lust after carefree summer vibes, “Sunshine” will warm and caress your heartstrings with utmost skill. Jungle perform at Climate Pledge Arena on October 3.

Led by cracked genius Arthur Lee, the LA band Love are best known for their 1966 single “7 and 7 Is,” a proto-punk flamethrower that belongs in every home, and for their 1967 LP Forever Changes , a beautifully acid-friend psych opus that consistently appears near the top of “best albums of all time” lists. However, Love’s less-beloved records have many gems, too, including 1970’s False Start , which has been out of print on vinyl for 56 years. My fave song on it is an anomaly in Love’s catalog; “Gimi a Little Break” starts like an homage to the Troggs’s “Wild Thing” (ask your grandmother) and then transforms into a euphoric glam-rock earworm, replete with serious cowbell and a scorching guitar solo. I also have a lot of time for any singer who stretches the word “shine” to five syllables.

Forty-two percent of those who lost coverage were “under 34, with black and Hispanic residents” bearing the brunt of white American Christianity.

Praise Father God, Amtrak Cascades will resume its service to Portland, the busiest part of its line in the Pacific Northwest , after a fire on August 2 threatened to collapse a warehouse onto the tracks near Union Station. The Seattle Times reports that trains will resume partial service today to Portland; the next day, all trains will carry the people to the great dives and strip clubs of Portlandia. Many of us feared it would take forever to revive the life of this crucial part of the line. But Lord, you showed us your mercy. Praise by thy name.
Trump has declared , on Truth Social , that the Strait of Hormuz is now “ NEW U.S. Territory. ”

What to make of this declaration of madness? It recalls the final scene of Werner Herzog’s Aguirre , the Wrath of God. But that conquistador, Gonzalo Pizarro (played with insane intensity by Klaus Kinski), wasn’t nearly as nuts as Trump at this point. Some of Pizarro’s declarations on the doomed ship, attacked by monkeys and indigenous arrows, proved to be correct. There is no such hope to expect from Trump’s drifting ship.

What Americans have to realize is the American Empire is now a thing of the past. If the US is lucky, it will continue as a tri-polar world: China, Europe, and North America. The last will require the US to open its borders to Canada and Mexico and create, possibly in Washington, D.C., a kind of Brussels . So sorry to say this, but American Awesome is now receding in the rearview mirror. Get used to it.

Recall that excellent line by the British R&B trio Loose Ends: “ It’s all a mystery to me .” The Seattle Times columnist Danny Westneat is somehow saying something similar about a river in Spokane that’s not “ rivering ”: “…for now [it’s] a mystery [to me].” On August 9, a mile of Spokane River went dry just like that. The same thing happened last year, and no one, not even scientists, has any idea why? Can I provide a clue, pretty please? In 2024 , the GOP candidates were all about that cheap gas; this time around, it’s the Democrats. No one in mainstream politics is saying no to gas. It’s only about its cost, which, in terms of social costs (the harm it does to the environment and humans), is way too cheap. If we wanted our dying rivers to rise and live again, we should be paying around $20 for a gallon. (By the way, the Spokesman-Review is not in the dark about what’s what . The Spokane River is dying because of climate change caused by capitalism. What is Westneat on?)

Speaking of rivers dying in the capitalocene (we must not call it the anthropocene because it blames humans in general and not a historically specific culture of humans, one that has as its substance the unlimited accumulation of value—and I use the word “substance” to mean that which is necessary for a certain thing to be a thing—for this climate catastrophe). Anyway, there appears to be no rain coming our way today. Expect a high of 79 today.

Creamed in Milwaukee: If Nathalie were here, and not on vacation at some reservoir, she would despair over the Mariners’ blowout loss to the Brewers 22-0 at American Family Field in Milwaukee. Never in franchise history have the M’s gotten their plump, juicy, brand-sponsored asses kicked this bad. According to the Seattle Times , 36,870 cheerful fans watched this torture scene, which began with the grim portent of a tornado warning.

Guys, the Mariners, I don’t know if you are reading this, but I know losing sucks. But losing really, really catastrophically bad— tying the MLB record for getting pantsed and stuffed into the proverbial locker , joining the Chicago Cubs and Cleveland Guardians New York Yankees*—is something else entirely. It is very funny. As your good friend and starting pitcher Bryce Miller said, y’all still have a chance at the Series. I have only this to say…

Since we’re talking disasters, the professional nerds at the Washington Department of Emergency Management, Department of Natural Resources, and others, modeled an Alaskan tsunami caused by a 9.2 quake along the Alaskan-Aluetian subduction zone—a much more likely scenario than the Big One—and found that a wall of water would indeed slam into our coastline, inundating our islands and charming beach towns with ferocious speed. What they didn’t expect to see were significant impacts on the inner coast of Puget Sound. At least folks would have more time to scramble up the hills in the event of an Alaskan quake than when the Cascadian subduction zone decides to do the tantarella. If you live in the drowning part of the state instead of the burning part of the state, experts urge you to find out how to receive emergency alerts . Also, get yourself a NOAA radio , which can be programmed to alert you to a tsunami’s presence.

Classes at California high school Wheatland Union were canceled yesterday after a bomb threat made by an AI-generated voice. “[This is] consistent with a pattern of hoax threats targeting schools across the country,” reports FOX40. Automated robo bomb threats have shut down schools in Georgia , in Vermont , and in Kansas .
UPDATE: Classes at Wheatland Union were delayed today after a second threat .
WIRED reconstructed Flock camera’s next-generation AI system for monitoring the Shiny Happy People of America and confirmed it does more than track license plates*.

“The software, originally called Nightshift and more recently renamed OS Investigate, ships with 69 prewritten prompts that officers can select, review, or edit, and then submit to the AI. Officers can also input prompts of their own.

The suggested prompts sit in a cache of more than 450 files that WIRED found on Flock’s own website, served by its login pages to anyone who loaded them. The code describes 45 tools at the AI’s disposal, giving it access to plate scans and camera metadata, arrest records, case files, dispatch logs, ballistics results, and commercial databases that contain Social Security numbers, dates of birth, phone numbers, email addresses, relatives and associates.”
*Freudian slip: Google Docs, which includes an annoying predictive text feature, autocompleted this sentence as “confirmed it does more harm than good.” Broken clocks.

Meanwhile, a Washington judge did her part for this technological revolution when she ruled that the Grant County Public Utility District can take land for data center power lines. Grant County Superior Court Judge Jennifer Richardson did not decide whether the utility had followed the “required negotiation and appraisal procedures,” reports the Times , but said it didn’t matter or invalidate the county’s decision to condemn nine properties in the way of the power lines. Unless the parties wave a jury, jurors will decide how much landowners will be paid. One plaintiff claims that Grant PUD valued her property $600,000 less than it was worth.

Frank Beard, the drummer of ZZ Top, and ironically, the trio’s only relatively clean-shaven member, joined the 77 club yesterday . Beard was in hospice care when he died at his ranch in Richland, Texas, not too far from the waterpark where I spent two blazing summers lifeguarding in high school. ZZ Top singer/guitarist Billy Gibbons said in a statement that he lost a true collaborator, and Texas lost a true son. A solemn yee haw.
To reflect, here’s Charles’s favorite ZZ tune: “Blue Jeans Blues.”

*Correction: Justin, a loyal reader and former Ohioan, let me know that, although he understands the concept of Cleveland as America’s punching bag, the Guardians beat the New York Yankees 22-0, not the other way around. “For what it’s worth, Cleveland beat the Yankees 22-0 in 2004, and it is that team from New York that shares the title with the Mariners for worst loss in baseball history. The Yankees already have the most championships and all the money, let’s at least recall their flaws accurately too.” Right you are, Justin. Thanks for your eagle, err, buckeye.

articles.title: All aboard Amtrak’s sleeker, cleaner new trains
articles.author: Benton Graham
paras: On Charlie Hamilton’s regular Amtrak rides from Seattle to Portland, Oregon, and Vancouver, British Columbia, he passes some of the country’s most spectacular vistas: the Puget Sound coast and the Skagit Valley. On clear days, he can even see Mount Rainier. But perhaps the most beautiful sight is not the natural wonders of the Pacific Northwest. It’s the cars and trucks inching along the highway.

“It’s nice to be able to be going along there and going faster than what people on Interstate 5 are doing. We kind of like that bit,” said Hamilton, who leads the train advocacy organization All Aboard Washington.

Indeed, riding the train in the Pacific Northwest can take about as long as driving. The trip between Seattle and Portland takes about 3 hours and 30 minutes by either mode, even though the train makes six stops along the way.

Amtrak plans to begin rolling out 83 new trainsets, dubbed Airo , this fall, starting with eight on the Pacific Northwest’s Cascades route. The trains will eventually serve more than a dozen routes in places like New England, Pennsylvania, and much of the mid-Atlantic region. The $8-billion investment is expected to reduce trip times on multiple routes, though Amtrak did not say by how much, and the trains can reach speeds of up to 125 mph. The Cascades trains will also carry 317 passengers — significantly more than the current Cascades rolling stock — and will boost reliability and comfort, according to an Amtrak spokesperson.

Improved hardware could also help advance All Aboard Washington’s vision of more frequent rail service in the region. “Having trains once an hour would be very helpful, and the Airo trainsets would make it possible to do that,” Hamilton said.

The Airo trains also represent a significant and long overdue refresh for Amtrak, which still has trains that date to the 1970s. The carrier has said the new hardware will provide “significant environmental benefits” while making the rider experience more pleasant. The rollout follows the introduction of new NextGen Acela trains on the Northeast Corridor last summer.

Amtrak’s refresh comes after the Biden administration made a historic $66 billion investment in passenger and freight rail through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. But it arrives at a tumultuous moment. Despite Amtrak setting ridership records for two consecutive years, the Trump administration has proposed severe cuts to passenger rail funding. Still, the federal government did announce $3 billion in funding, including $2 billion to purchase trains, for Amtrak in August.

Rail carries 8 percent of the world’s passengers, yet accounts for just 2 percent of global transportation energy demand. In that sense, the Airo trains will help make a clean form of transport even cleaner.

Alex Scott, a professor of supply chain management at the University of Tennessee-Knoxville, said rail’s efficiency comes in part from carrying many people at once. “If you can get a fully well-utilized rail car, be it humans or products, those are still more efficient than everybody going in different cars, even if they’re electric cars,” he said.

The trains, built in the U.S. by Siemens , feature electric and diesel propulsion, allowing them to operate on both conventional and electrified routes. While much of the U.S. passenger rail network remains unelectrified, employing new diesel-powered trains can still reduce emissions. “The locomotives they make now, even if they’re not electric, are a heck of a lot cleaner than the old ones, and so upgrading equipment, be it electric or not, is a good answer,” Scott said.

Airo locomotives meet the Environmental Protection Agency’s Tier 4 emissions standards — the agency’s strictest rules for locomotive engines — significantly reducing particulate matter and nitrogen oxide emissions.

Riders on the Northeast Regional route will climb aboard Airo trains in 2027. The new rolling stock will especially benefit riders traveling between Virginia and the Northeast who can wait as long as an hour at Union Station in Washington, D.C. while Amtrak swaps the diesel engine it uses south of the capital to the electric one it uses northbound to Boston. The new trains can quickly transition from diesel to electric power without changing locomotives.

“It’s a win for the environment, it’s a win for the people that are sitting in traffic,” Virginia Passenger Rail Authority spokesperson Karina Romero said. “We definitely want more trains in Virginia.”

Virginia has invested $6 billion in its Transforming Rail in Virginia program. According to Romero, the combination of new trains and improved infrastructure will give riders a more reliable experience.
“You can put down fabulous infrastructure and great tracks,” she said, “but you’ve definitely got to have the equipment to roll on.”
This story was originally published by Grist with the headline All aboard Amtrak’s sleeker, cleaner new trains on Aug 19, 2026.

articles.title: Did someone wearing Meta Glasses film you today? Are you sure?
articles.author: Maggie Harrison Dupré
paras: People say they’ve been secretly filmed in their own homes, at concerts and at work. Are the wildly popular smartglasses the final nail in the coffin of personal privacy?

“I’ve had one person who told me that their intentions were creepy,” a man tells me over a video call, on condition of anonymity. He’s based in Los Angeles, and while we speak, he eats what appears to be tuna directly out of the can. “He said: ‘I go to strip clubs, and I want to record the strippers … Normally I put my phone in my chest pocket, but the glasses are more convenient.’”

The man I’m talking to runs a business called Ghost Metas . He’s one of hundreds of vendors, easily discoverable online, who specialise in disabling the flashing LED light embedded in Meta’s smartglasses that blinks when wearers capture photos, videos and audio. After Ghost Metas disables the LED, it’s impossible for someone to know they’re being filmed.

articles.title: Nearly 1 in 4 students are chronically absent from school – kids who feel happy and safe are less likely to miss class
articles.author:
<name>Jerome A. Graham, Assistant Professor of K-12 Educational Administration, Michigan State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jerome-a-graham-2750457"/>
paras: Chronic absenteeism – referring to students who miss 10% or more days of the school year – has become one of the most urgent problems across American schools since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Before the pandemic, about 15% of students across the country missed that much school.
That figure roughly doubled between 2022 and 2023 to more than 28%, according to recent national estimates.
Now, several years later, this figure sits at around 23% nationally. That means close to 1 in 4 students are still missing enough school to put their learning at serious risk.
Researchers point to various challenges to help explain why so many students frequently miss school , including poverty, unreliable transportation and housing instability.
But addressing those problems requires long-term policy changes that are often slow to make and not necessarily possible.

This challenge layered on top of the very real barriers that chronically absent students face can make educators feel defeated and think that absenteeism is simply too big and entrenched of a problem for schools to meaningfully address. This feeling can cause educators and other observers to lose sight of how the school itself can be part of the solution.

We are education scholars who recently published research showing that positive school climates play a significant role in reducing chronic absenteeism, including for students most at risk for chronic absence. This research demonstrates that when schools attend to the conditions that make all students feel welcomed and valued, they are much more likely to show up.
How students feel at school plays a more consequential role in reducing rates of chronic absenteeism than some might think.
Our January 2026 analysis draws on nearly a decade of data from the Georgia Student Health Survey , an annual survey the state conducts with middle and high school students.
We found that school climate – or how students experience their schools on a day-to-day basis – matters a lot for whether they attend school regularly.

A school’s climate is shaped by whether students feel safe, whether they feel they belong, whether there are adults who know them and support them, and whether the building runs in a way that helps them learn. In other words, it’s how school feels to the students inside it – and as these experiences become more positive, students are much less likely to miss a lot of school.
In 2021, a study of New York City students reached similar conclusions, as did another 2026 study of Chicago students .
These researchers found that school climate and how connected students felt to their school mattered even more for attendance after the pandemic than before it.

Across very different contexts – even after accounting for poverty, homelessness and other factors that contribute to chronic absence – these studies suggest that when students feel safe, connected and supported at school, they show up.

But our results from Georgia reveal something equally important about what happens when schools lose that positive climate. When students perceive their school becoming less welcoming and supportive, their absences don’t just increase gradually – they spike dramatically. And these spikes are steepest among Black and Latino students.
When we look at what schools are actually doing to improve attendance, a revealing gap emerges.
Some school leaders are clearly taking the problem seriously.

Nearly half of surveyed school principals in Georgia and Michigan named attendance as a top concern in a 2025 survey. These principals said they were trying a range of responses to address the problem.

However, most of their strategies were either communication-based, such as calling or writing to parents, or incentives-based, such as offering rewards to students for good attendance. While potentially helpful, these approaches are aimed at changing student or parent behavior but do little to address some other underlying reasons students are missing school, such as school climate.
This same survey finds that in both states, strategies focused on improving what students actually experience inside the building make up only about 15% of what schools report doing.

When we look more closely at which specific dimensions of climate appear to matter most for reducing absenteeism, three stood out as the most consequential. They were connectedness, safety, and structure for learning.

Connectedness reflects whether students feel a sense of belonging and feel tied to others at school. Of the eight school climate dimensions included in our analysis, connectedness was the strongest predictor, corresponding to nearly a 3 percentage point reduction in chronic absenteeism.

Safety, meaning an environment where students are not worried about being hurt or caught up in frequent conflict, was similarly linked to notable declines in chronic absence. Structure for learning, or whether a school has clear systems and supports in place, including consistent behavioral standards and high academic expectations, also predicted meaningful declines in the share of chronically absent students.

Importantly, these patterns held across both middle and high schools and across racial groups, which suggests that investing in these areas is a broadly applicable strategy for making school a place students want to be.

Creating a welcoming school climate requires real work. It asks school leaders and teachers to both acknowledge the challenges that make school harder for some students and honestly ask: Are we inviting students in or pushing them away?

A school might start small. We think that auditing who is being suspended and for what, making sure every student has at least one adult checking in on them, or asking students directly what would make them want to be at school are all good places to begin.
Poverty, transportation and housing instability are real barriers to students’ attendance, and we believe that addressing them remains essential. But fixing these challenges will take time.

When educators and school administrators prioritize whether students feel connected to their school community, as well as safe and supported at school, they send students a message that is itself an intervention: You are seen here, you are safe here, and this place was built with you in mind. Our data suggests that message is powerful enough to help bring some students back.
